title: The Armband
part: PART THREE: THE HIGH AND THE HOLE

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #40: Take off the armband and hope somebody asks you to put it back on.*

Thursday smells like rain and wet asphalt. I leave the yellow armband on the bench. I do not say goodbye, nor do I look back. I simply peel it off my arm, where it has lived for twelve weeks, and set it on the plastic seat next to Ollie’s bag of orange slices. It looks heavy there. It looks like a dead thing.

I walk to the bike rack, my legs feeling as if they are filled with wet sand. I ride home, eat a single cracker, and ride back out. The sun is setting, turning the sky the color of a bruised peach. I ride to the bus depot.

The old yellow bus is parked in the shade. It is quiet. I open the driver’s side door and climb up the steps to sit in the doorway. The metal is cold against my legs. I am not a captain, nor a player. I am a girl with an own goal, a statistic, a video.

I put my head in my hands and wait for the feeling to go away. It does not. It sits in my chest, heavy and warm, like a rock that has been sitting in a pocket for too long.
pages.image: A wiry 12-year-old girl with a high dark ponytail and yellow elastic sits alone in the open doorway of an big blank yellow minibus, head in hands, at dusk; empty parking lot, wet asphalt, quiet mood.

pages.text:
Footsteps crunch on the gravel behind me, though I keep my eyes fixed on the yellow paint peeling off the bus bumper. The door creaks open, flooding the entryway with the sharp, bitter scent of strong tea, probably Earl Grey or something even worse.

"Rafael’s daughter," a voice says. Calm. Flat.

I lift my head to find Coach Gin standing there in her fluorescent windbreaker, holding two mugs. She hands me the ceramic one, which burns my fingers until I have to hold it like a slice of toast left too long on the stove. Then she simply says, "Sit."

She climbs the steps and lowers herself onto the edge of the doorway next to me. Her knees knock against the wheel well before she takes a sip and immediately spits it out.

"Too strong," I manage to say.

"Good. It wakes you up."

She looks out at the empty lot, her silver braid swinging slightly as she turns her head. "I drove a school bus for thirty-eight years," she tells me. "Forty-one kids most mornings. Screaming. Throwing up. Dropping their lunch on the seat. Nobody ever asked me for the score. Nobody ever asked if I had won."

She sips again, and this time she doesn't flinch. "I lost things I loved. My husband. My job. My youth. None of them were games. But they hurt just the same."
pages.image: A short, square woman with a silver braid and sunglasses on her head sits on the big blank yellow minibus step next to a 12-year-old girl; she holds a ceramic mug; both look out at the dusk-lit parking lot; calm, quiet mood.

pages.text:
I drink the tea. It tastes like dirt and lemon, which is terrible, and also perfect. "I don't know who I am without a win," I say. My voice sounds small, like it is coming from someone else.

Gin nods without looking at me. She stares at the bus key on her lanyard instead. "That is the most honest sentence you have said all season," she says. "Now we know what we are working on."

She holds out her palm without a word. I dig into my sock and find the card, soft and curved from three weeks against my ankle bone, and I hand it over. She reads the front. On the front, in my shaky handwriting, is one word: captain. The back is blank.

"What did you do well against the Hawks?" she asks.

"Nothing," I say.

"Try again," she says.

I stare at the card, and the word captain looks back at me like it is mocking me. I feel my face heat up, and I want to put my head back in my hands and disappear.
pages.image: A 12-year-old girl with brown skin and a yellow armband held loosely in her hand sits in a big blank yellow minibus doorway; a short woman with a silver braid holds a small white card; the girl looks down at the card with a sad, defensive expression; evening light, quiet interior.

pages.text:
The sky goes dark, and the streetlights buzz on with a sound like a mosquito trapped in a jar. They look ugly at this hour. Like broken teeth.

My mind wanders to the Hawks, then the field, then Tank. He is huge, but he is always exactly where he needs to be.

"I saw where Tank was going to be," I say. My voice is quiet. Steady. "I was already on the ball. I just didn't pass."

Gin makes a low sound in her throat. "Mm."

"I see the field before it happens," I say, the words tumbling out fast like marbles from a jar. "I always have. I just never counted it because it doesn't show up on the board."

I look down at the card. It is still white and blank, but it feels different now, like a heavy door waiting to be pushed open. I can almost hear the handle turn.

My fingers find my pencil in my pocket. It is short, worn down to a tiny nub, just like my eraser when I was in fourth grade. I unscrew the cap and reveal the sharp, black lead.
pages.image: A 12-year-old girl with a high ponytail sits in a big blank yellow minibus doorway at night, holding a white card and a short pencil; a streetlight glows behind her; she looks focused and serious; dark blue night sky, big blank yellow minibus paint.

pages.text:
The pencil scratches against the paper with a sound like a mouse sprinting across a shingled roof. I look down at what I just wrote. The words are small, but they hold weight.

I read the sentence twice. Then a third time. It is true. It belongs to me, not the scoreboard. It doesn't care about Carter Boyle’s video or the crowd’s silence. It is just me, the field, and the empty space between the players.

I fold the card up tight and tuck it into my sock, where it settles warm and solid against my ankle. It feels like a secret kept safe in a shoe locker.

Gin taps the door frame with one knuckle. "It will be there," she says, nodding toward the bench, three miles away. "But first, you owe somebody an apology. And it isn’t me."

She stands up, places her steel mug back in the bus cupholder, and looks down at me. Her eyes are sharp, but they are soft underneath.

"Go home, Dani," she says. "Eat something. And fix what you broke."

I nod, my legs shaking a little, though they are still my own. I climb down the steps into the cold night air.
pages.image: A 12-year-old girl with a high ponytail and yellow armband stands at the base of a big blank yellow minibus step, looking up at a short woman with a silver braid; the woman holds a steel mug; night scene, streetlight glow, serious but hopeful mood.
